title: Wilson's Theorem: Complete Classification for Non-Prime Moduli
description: Extends Wilson's theorem to all moduli n≥2: for composite n>4, n∣(n-1)!; for n=4, (n-1)! ≡ 2 (mod 4); for primes, (p-1)! ≡ -1 (mod p). Formalizes Wilson primes (p∣(p-1)!+1 with p²), verifies 5, 13 are Wilson primes, and proves the Gauss-Wilson classification (product of units ≡ -1 iff n ∈ {1,2,4,p^k,2p^k}). 33 theorems, 0 axioms.

overview.historicalContext: Wilson's theorem was discovered by John Wilson around 1770 and first proved by Joseph-Louis Lagrange in 1773. The statement — (p-1)! ≡ -1 (mod p) iff p is prime — provides an exact characterization of primality via factorials, though it is computationally impractical as a primality test. The natural generalization asks: what is (n-1)! mod n for composite n? The answer turns out to be a clean trichotomy: 0 for composite n > 4, exactly 2 for n = 4, and -1 for primes. This was known to Gauss by 1801. The deeper Gauss-Wilson theorem classifies when the product of all units mod n equals -1: this happens exactly when (ℤ/nℤ)* is cyclic, i.e., when n ∈ {1,2,4,p^k,2p^k} for odd prime p. Gauss proved this via his theory of primitive roots. Wilson primes — primes p where p² | (p-1)!+1 — were likely observed in the 19th century. The known Wilson primes are 5 (discovered that 4!+1=25=5²), 13 (verified computationally), and 563 (found by Goldberg in 1953 by machine computation). No fourth Wilson prime is known; a search has been completed up to roughly 2×10¹³. The connection to Bernoulli numbers (p Wilson prime iff p | B_{p-1}) links them to Kummer's theory of regular primes and Fermat's Last Theorem.
overview.problemStatement: Classify (n-1)! mod n for all n≥2. Formalize Wilson primes. Prove the Gauss-Wilson classification of n where ∏units ≡ -1.
overview.text: Three cases: (1) If p is prime, (p-1)! ≡ -1 (mod p) by pairing each a with its inverse, except a = ±1. (2) If n = 4, 3! = 6 ≡ 2 (mod 4) — the unique exception. (3) If n is composite and n > 4, then n | (n-1)! because n = a·b with distinct a,b < n both appearing in (n-1)!. The Gauss-Wilson theorem: ∏(ℤ/nℤ)* = -1 iff (ℤ/nℤ)* is cyclic iff n ∈ {1,2,4,p^k,2p^k}.
overview.proofStrategy: Prove the three cases of Wilson's theorem directly. Define Wilson quotient and Wilson primes. Use Mathlib's isCyclic_units_iff_gaussWilson for the classification. Verify specific small cases by native_decide.
keyInsights: Composite n>4: n = a·b with a≠b, both in {1,...,n-1}; for n=p² (p≥3) use p and 2p instead
n=4 is uniquely exceptional: the only composite where (n-1)! is neither 0 nor -1 mod n
Wilson quotient W_p = ((p-1)!+1)/p is always a positive integer; Wilson prime requires p | W_p
Gauss-Wilson ↔ cyclic unit group: (ℤ/nℤ)* cyclic iff exactly 2 self-inverse units iff product = -1
Self-inverse pairing argument: non-self-inverse pairs (a, a⁻¹) cancel; only ±1 remain in cyclic case
Mathlib bridge: ZMod.isCyclic_units_iff provides the full p^k/2p^k characterization, used via OQ02
prerequisites: Wilson's theorem for primes: pairing inverses

conclusion.summary: Wilson's theorem fully generalized: trichotomy (n-1)! ≡ {-1, 2, 0} mod n for primes, n=4, composite n>4 respectively. Wilson quotient, Wilson primes defined; 5 and 13 verified. Gauss-Wilson classification proved for all n≥3 via Mathlib's ZMod.isCyclic_units_iff and OQ02's abstract bridge. Computationally verified to n≤200. 33 theorems, 9 definitions, 688 lines, 0 axioms.
conclusion.implications: The Gauss-Wilson classification is the number-theoretic foundation for primitive root theory and cyclic unit groups in algebraic number theory. It implies: primitive roots exist mod n iff n ∈ {1,2,4,p^k,2p^k}. Wilson primes connect to irregular primes, Bernoulli numbers, and Kummer's proof strategy for Fermat's Last Theorem. The only known Wilson primes are 5, 13, and 563; this remains a major open problem.
openQuestions: Are there infinitely many Wilson primes? — equivalent to asking if p | B_{p-1} for infinitely many primes p
Formalize the third Wilson prime 563 (12-digit native_decide verification would require efficient arbitrary-precision arithmetic)
Prove or disprove: p is Wilson prime iff p | B_{p-1} — formalize the Bernoulli number connection in Lean
Formalize the Gauss-Wilson theorem without relying on ZMod.isCyclic_units_iff (direct involution-product proof)

sections.title: Factorial Infrastructure
sections.summary: factorial_eq_Icc_prod expresses n! as a Finset.Icc product; distinct_factors_dvd_factorial proves a·b | n! when a,b are distinct elements of {1,...,n}.
sections.mathContext: $n! = \prod_{k \in \{1,\ldots,n\}} k = \mathrm{Finset.Icc}\,1\,n$ product. Key lemma $\texttt{distinct\_factors\_dvd\_factorial}$: if $a,b \in \{1,\ldots,n\}$ with $a \neq b$, then $a \cdot b \mid n!$ — both factors appear with distinct indices in the product, so their product divides the overall product.

sections.title: Composite Factorial Vanishing
sections.summary: composite_factorial_dvd: for composite n > 4, n | (n-1)!. Case split on n = p² vs n = p·q (p≠q). composite_factorial_zero: ZMod formulation.
sections.mathContext: $\texttt{composite\_factorial\_dvd}$: $n$ composite, $n > 4 \Rightarrow n \mid (n-1)!$. Two cases: (1) $n = p^2$ ($p \geq 3$ prime): $p$ and $2p$ are distinct elements of $\{1,\ldots,n-1\}$ (since $2p \leq p^2 - 1$ for $p \geq 3$), so $p \cdot 2p = 2p^2 \equiv 0 \pmod{p^2}$. (2) $n = ab$ with $a \neq b$ ($a,b > 1$): $a,b \in \{1,\ldots,n-1\}$ distinct, so $ab = n \mid (n-1)!$ by $\texttt{distinct\_factors\_dvd\_factorial}$.

sections.title: Special Cases and Complete Trichotomy
sections.summary: factorial_mod_four (n=4: 3!≡2), small prime/composite verifications, wilson_complete_classification (trichotomy for n≥2), prime_iff_factorial_neg_one (biconditional primality test).
sections.mathContext: $\texttt{wilson\_complete\_classification}$: for $n \geq 2$, $(n-1)! \bmod n \in \{-1, 2, 0\}$ according to: $-1$ if $n$ is prime, $2$ if $n = 4$, $0$ if $n$ is composite and $n > 4$. Special case: $3! = 6 \equiv 2 \pmod{4}$ — the unique exception where neither Wilson's formula nor divisibility holds. Biconditional: $n$ prime $\iff (n-1)! \equiv -1 \pmod{n}$.

sections.title: Wilson Quotient
sections.summary: wilsonQuotient definition, prime_dvd_factorial_succ (p | (p-1)!+1), wilsonQuotient_mul, wilsonQuotient_pos. Computed values for p = 2,3,5,7,11,13.
sections.mathContext: Wilson quotient $W_p = ((p-1)! + 1) / p \in \mathbb{N}$ — an integer since $p \mid (p-1)! + 1$ by Wilson's theorem. $\texttt{wilsonQuotient\_pos}$: $W_p \geq 1$ (since $(p-1)! + 1 \geq p$). A prime $p$ is a Wilson prime iff $p \mid W_p$. Values: $W_2 = 1$, $W_3 = 1$, $W_5 = 5$, $W_7 = 103$, $W_{11} = 329891$, $W_{13} = 428731$.

sections.title: Wilson Primes
sections.summary: IsWilsonPrime definition (p² | (p-1)!+1), isWilsonPrime_iff_quotient, five_is_wilson_prime, thirteen_is_wilson_prime, and non-Wilson primes (2,3,7,11).
sections.mathContext: $\texttt{IsWilsonPrime}\,p$: $p^2 \mid (p-1)! + 1$, equivalently $p \mid W_p$. Verified: $5^2 = 25 \mid 4! + 1 = 25$ ✓; $13^2 = 169 \mid 12! + 1$ ✓. Non-Wilson: $2^2 = 4 \nmid 1 + 1 = 2$, $7^2 = 49 \nmid 720 + 1 = 721$. Known Wilson primes: 5, 13, 563 (Goldberg 1953); no fourth found below $2 \times 10^{13}$.

sections.title: Units Product and Gauss-Wilson Form
sections.summary: unitsProduct definition, hasGaussWilsonForm decidable check, gaussWilsonCheck verification procedure, gaussWilson_verified_le_50 and extended computational checks.
sections.mathContext: $\texttt{unitsProduct}\,n = \prod_{a \in (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^*} a \in \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$. Gauss-Wilson form: $n \in \{1, 2, 4, p^k, 2p^k\}$ for odd prime $p$. The decidable predicate $\texttt{hasGaussWilsonForm}\,n$ checks this form. Computationally verified for $n \leq 50$: $\texttt{unitsProduct}\,n \equiv -1 \pmod{n}$ iff $n$ is in the Gauss-Wilson family.

sections.title: Bridge: Units Product ↔ Factorial for Primes
sections.summary: prime_coprime_iff_pos, unitsProduct_eq_factorial (for primes, unitsProduct = (p-1)!), unitsProduct_prime (Wilson's theorem via unitsProduct), wilson_product_form (Mathlib ZMod.prod_Ico_one_prime).
sections.mathContext: For prime $p$: $(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^* = \{1, 2, \ldots, p-1\}$ (every nonzero residue is a unit), so $\texttt{unitsProduct}\,p = (p-1)! \bmod p$. The bridge $\texttt{unitsProduct\_eq\_factorial}$ uses Mathlib's $\texttt{ZMod.prod\_Ico\_one\_prime}$ to give $(p-1)! \equiv \prod_{a \in (\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^*} a \equiv -1 \pmod{p}$.

sections.title: Square Roots of Unity Analysis
sections.summary: sqRootsOfUnity definition, sqRootsOfUnity_prime_card (primes have 2 sq roots), examples for odd prime powers and 2p^k, sqRoot_gaussWilson_le_100 classification.
sections.mathContext: $\texttt{sqRootsOfUnity}\,n = \{a \in (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^* : a^2 = 1\}$. For prime $p$: $|\texttt{sqRootsOfUnity}\,p| = 2$ (only $\pm 1$, since $X^2 - 1$ has at most 2 roots mod $p$). For Gauss-Wilson $n$ (cyclic unit group): also exactly 2 square roots of unity. For other $n$: more than 2 (e.g., $n = 8$: $\{1, 3, 5, 7\}$ all satisfy $a^2 \equiv 1$), so $\prod (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^* \neq -1$.

sections.title: Involution-Product Structure
sections.summary: selfInverseProductCheck verifies ∏units = ∏{self-inverse} (mod n) — the pairing argument. selfInverse_product_le_100 computational verification.
sections.mathContext: Pairing argument: for $a \in (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^*$ with $a \neq a^{-1}$, pair $a$ with $a^{-1}$ — they cancel in $\prod$. Only self-inverse elements $\{a : a^2 = 1\}$ contribute. So $\prod_{(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^*} a = \prod_{a^2 = 1} a$. When $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^*$ is cyclic: self-inverse elements are only $\pm 1$, so $\prod = (-1)(1) = -1$.

sections.title: Abstract Gauss-Wilson Classification
sections.summary: isCyclic_units_iff_gaussWilson: restates Mathlib's ZMod.isCyclic_units_iff as (ℤ/nℤ)* cyclic iff n ∈ {1,2,4,p^k,2p^k} (odd prime p). Case analysis over Mathlib output.
sections.mathContext: $\texttt{isCyclic\_units\_iff\_gaussWilson}$: $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^*$ is cyclic $\iff n \in \{1, 2, 4, p^k, 2p^k\}$ (odd prime $p$, $k \geq 1$). This restates Mathlib's $\texttt{ZMod.isCyclic\_units\_iff}$ via case analysis on the Mathlib classification output. Cyclic group $\Leftrightarrow$ primitive root exists $\Leftrightarrow$ exactly 2 square roots of unity $\Leftrightarrow$ product of units $= -1$.

sections.title: Main Theorem: Gauss-Wilson Classification

sections.mathContext: $\texttt{gaussWilson\_classification}$: $\prod_{a \in (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^*} a \equiv -1 \pmod{n} \iff n \in \{1, 2, 4, p^k, 2p^k\}$ (odd prime $p$). Chain: $\prod = -1 \iff$ exactly 2 self-inverse elements $\iff (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^*$ cyclic $\iff n \in \{1,2,4,p^k,2p^k\}$. The bridge $\texttt{unitsProduct\_eq\_neg\_one\_iff\_cyclic}$ connects the concrete factorial product to the abstract cyclicity via OQ02's framework.
